title: Weaken to Strengthen: Weakening-Induced On-Policy Self-Distillation for Large Reasoning Models

paper.title: Weaken to Strengthen: Weakening-Induced On-Policy Self-Distillation for Large Reasoning Models
paper.abstract:
Abstract Self-distillation offers a way to improve reasoning models when a suitable
external teacher is unavailable.
However, common approaches rely on privileged information to construct a
stronger self-teacher, limiting their use when only unlabeled prompts are
available.
In this paper, we introduce Weakening-Induced On-Policy Self-Distillation (WISD), which instead
constructs a weaker counterpart of the original model and uses the contrast
between the two as a training signal without requiring privileged information.
We explore two ways to construct the weaker model: low-bit quantization and
magnitude pruning.
We evaluate WISD across diverse architectures and scales on mathematical and coding reasoning tasks.
Across these benchmarks, quantization and pruning improve average
accuracy over the original models by 4.0 and 5.5 percentage points,
respectively, achieving state-of-the-art performance even without privileged information.
Notably, pruning raises Qwen3.5-4B’s accuracy from 57.7% to 70.5% on
HMMT 2025 and from 39.1% to 56.7% on LiveCodeBench v6.
Quantization raises Qwen3.6-35B-A3B’s accuracy from 68.5% to 74.6% and from
61.8% to 69.5% on the same benchmarks, respectively.
These results establish WISD as a novel and effective self-distillation
framework for large reasoning models. Code is released at https://github.com/jet-ai-projects/WISD .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: On-policy distillation (OPD) has emerged as an effective approach to improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2024 ; Lu and Lab, 2025 ) . It trains a student on its own generated trajectories using dense token-level supervision from a teacher, combining learning on the student’s own states with fine-grained feedback. For reasoning tasks, this allows learning to address errors in intermediate computations and decisions along the student’s own solution paths. This approach has demonstrated substantial gains in training efficiency and is now used in the post-training of Qwen3, MiMo-V2-Flash, Nemotron-Cascade 2, and DeepSeek-V4 ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Team et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026d ; DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026 ) . Recent work extends OPD to self-distillation, in which the same model serves as both teacher and student, removing the need for a separate teacher model ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Shenfeld et al., 2026 ; Hübotter et al., 2026 ) . Self-distillation is particularly appealing when a suitable external teacher is unavailable, especially when the goal is to improve an already capable model ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ) . A common approach uses the model’s in-context learning ability to construct a stronger teacher by providing privileged information, such as reference solutions ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) , expert demonstrations ( Shenfeld et al., 2026 ) , or textual environment feedback ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ) . With this additional context, the teacher can provide more informed predictions for trajectories that the student generates from the task input alone. Training matches the student’s next-token distributions to the teacher’s, transferring the benefit of the richer context into a policy that operates without privileged information at inference time. However, these approaches retain a dependence on privileged information during training. Reference-based methods require solutions or expert demonstrations ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Shenfeld et al., 2026 ) , and obtaining high-quality solutions can be costly ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) . Feedback-based alternatives rely on informative environment responses or reward-verified successful rollouts ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ) . These requirements limit their applicability when only unlabeled prompts are available. Even when privileged information is available, conditioning on it can shift the teacher’s predictions away from the student’s and complicate knowledge transfer ( Penaloza et al., 2026 ) . This motivates our central question: Can a model improve its reasoning through self-distillation without privileged information? Recent work on weak-to-strong OPD shows that the log-probability contrast between paired models can provide useful supervision even when both are weaker than the student ( Feng et al., 2026 ; Yu et al., 2026 ) . Differences in token preferences between paired models encode a direction of policy improvement that can be transferred to a more capable student. From this perspective, the privileged-information approaches above take the model itself as the weaker member of a pair and construct a stronger counterpart through additional context ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Shenfeld et al., 2026 ; Hübotter et al., 2026 ) . We introduce Weakening-Induced On-Policy Self-Distillation (WISD), which reverses this construction: we take the original model as the stronger member and create a weaker counterpart by degrading its weights. The contrast between the original model and its weakened copy then provides dense supervision on the model’s own trajectories, without privileged information. This formulation turns model weakening into a source of supervision, enabling self-improvement using the original model and unlabeled task prompts alone. Table 1 compares WISD with representative reasoning post-training methods in terms of learning signals and external supervision requirements. Table 1 : Comparison of training methods for reasoning. WISD provides dense supervision without external teachers, reference solutions, or environment feedback. Reference solutions are externally supplied answers or worked solutions used as teacher context. Environment feedback includes outcome verification and textual responses. GRPO uses verifiable outcome rewards. SDPO uses textual feedback or reward-verified self-generated solutions. Both operate directly on model weights and require no calibration data. Experiments across diverse model architectures and scales demonstrate the effectiveness of WISD on mathematical and coding reasoning tasks. Figure 1 summarizes the gains in mathematical and coding reasoning. Across these benchmarks, quantization and pruning improve average accuracy over the original models by 4.0 and 5.5 percentage points, respectively, with positive gains in 21 and 23 of the 25 model–benchmark settings, achieving state-of-the-art performance even without privileged information. Notably, pruning raises Qwen3.5-4B’s accuracy from 57.7% to 70.5% on HMMT 2025 and from 39.1% to 56.7% on LiveCodeBench v6. Quantization raises Qwen3.6-35B-A3B’s accuracy from 68.5% to 74.6% and from 61.8% to 69.5% on the same benchmarks, respectively. These results establish WISD as a novel and effective self-distillation framework for large reasoning models, requiring minimal prerequisites. Our contributions are as follows: • We introduce WISD, a self-distillation approach that treats the original model as the stronger member of a pair and learns from its contrast with a weakened copy, improving reasoning without privileged information. • We instantiate this approach with two weak-model constructions, low-bit quantization and magnitude pruning, which require no calibration data and yield dense supervision on the model’s own trajectories. • We validate the approach across widely used reasoning models spanning diverse architectures and scales, demonstrating broad accuracy improvements on mathematical and coding reasoning tasks.

sections.heading: On-Policy Distillation.
sections.text: On-policy distillation trains a student on its own generated trajectories ( Li et al., 2026b ; Fu et al., 2026 ; Ruan et al., 2026 ) with token-level teacher feedback ( Jin et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Armandpour et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026b ) , reducing the distribution mismatch between training and inference ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2024 ; Lu and Lab, 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026b ; Xu et al., 2025 ) . Direct On-Policy Distillation (DOPD) and related approaches transfer policy shifts through log-probability contrasts between paired models ( Yang et al., 2026b ; Feng et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026c ) , enabling weak-to-strong distillation ( Yu et al., 2026 ) . A growing line of work extends OPD to self-distillation by conditioning the model itself on additional information to obtain a stronger teacher: reference solutions ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Ke et al., 2026 ; Shen et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026a ) , demonstrations ( Shenfeld et al., 2026 ) , and environment feedback or verified successful rollouts ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ; Tan and Hong, 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026c ; He et al., 2026 ; Sun et al., 2026 ) . Compared to these prior self-distillation approaches, WISD requires no privileged information. Instead, it constructs a weaker copy of the original model and uses the contrast between the two as the training signal. OPSA takes a complementary approach, constructing entropy-adaptive negative advantages without an external teacher or privileged information ( Ding and Zhang, 2026 ) .

sections.heading: Learning from Weaker Models.
sections.text: Contrasting a model with a weaker counterpart has been explored for both generation ( Shi et al., 2024 ; Hong et al., 2023 ; Ahn et al., 2025 ) and learning. Contrastive decoding uses a smaller amateur to guide a stronger expert at inference time ( Li et al., 2023 ; O’Brien and Lewis, 2023 ) . Variants derive weaker predictions from the model itself ( Gera et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Jiang et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) through early layers in DoLa ( Chuang et al., 2024 ) , dropout or quantization in DCD ( Phan et al., 2024 ) , and layer pruning in PruneCD ( Yu et al., 2025 ) . Related small-model contrasts support decoding-time adaptation ( Mitchell et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) . In diffusion, classifier-free guidance contrasts conditional and unconditional predictions ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) , while autoguidance uses a smaller, less-trained counterpart ( Karras et al., 2024 ) . Training-time approaches include pruned self-competitors for visual representation learning ( Jiang et al., 2021 ) and expert–amateur contrasts for reasoning supervision ( Wang et al., 2026a ) . Recent distillation methods construct degraded references for flow-matching models ( Lin et al., 2026 ) or reduce expert activation in an external MoE teacher to obtain a reference ( Gu et al., 2026 ) . Self-distillation also exploits predictions conditioned on ablated visual inputs ( Liang et al., 2026 ) or self-generated negative context ( Pei et al., 2026 ) . WISD constructs a weaker counterpart directly through training-free weight quantization or magnitude pruning and distills its contrast with the original model to improve reasoning without privileged information.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: We first review OPD and policy-shift supervision, then revisit self-distillation from a weak-to-strong perspective to introduce WISD. Finally, we describe two training-free ways to construct its weaker model. Figure 2 contrasts WISD with prior self-distillation and summarizes its training pipeline. Figure 2 : Overview of WISD. (a) Prior self-distillation. Privileged information c c , such as solutions, demonstrations, or feedback, strengthens the original model into a self-teacher. (b) WISD. We instead retain the original model as the stronger member and construct a weaker copy through training-free quantization or pruning. The frozen pair scores the same self-generated trajectories, and its token-level log-probability contrast provides cached supervision for a student initialized from the original model, without privileged information.

sections.heading: 3.2 Weakening-Induced On-Policy Self-Distillation
sections.text: Weak-to-strong distillation suggests that a useful supervision signal can come from the difference between two models, even when a stronger teacher is unavailable ( Yu et al., 2026 ) . The central design choice is therefore how to obtain a model pair whose relative predictions provide a learning signal. This paired-model perspective also offers a way to understand prior on-policy self-distillation (OPSD). Given a model π \pi and privileged information c c , these approaches construct a more informed self-teacher π ( ⋅ ∣ s , c ) \pi(\cdot\mid s,c) using reference solutions ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) , demonstrations ( Shenfeld et al., 2026 ) , or environment feedback ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ) . These operators introduce two different forms of degradation: quantization coarsens weight values, while pruning removes low-magnitude connections. Both retain the model’s architecture and tokenizer, making their next-token predictions directly comparable to those of the original model. The transformations apply to attention and feed-forward projection weights, including MoE expert projections. Embeddings, output heads, normalization parameters, and routing parameters are preserved. The transformation is applied only to the frozen weak scorer. The student retains the original weights at initialization. For each projection matrix W W , we divide every output row into groups G G of 128 128 input columns and write M G = max j ∈ G ⁡ | W i ​ j | M_{G}=\max_{j\in G}|W_{ij}| .

sections.heading: Models and weakening variants.
sections.text: We evaluate WISD on five reasoning models: Qwen3-4B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , Qwen3.5-4B ( Qwen Team, 2026a ) , OLMo-3-7B-Think ( Team Olmo et al., 2026 ) , Qwen3.6-27B ( Qwen Team, 2026b ) , and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B ( Qwen Team, 2026c ) . These models span diverse sizes, families, and attention architectures, covering both dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) designs. For each model, we compare the original checkpoint with students trained using the quantization and pruning constructions in Section 3.3 , denoted by WISD (Quantization) and WISD (Pruning). The main results use b = 3 b=3 for quantization and τ = 1 / 6 \tau=1/6 for pruning. Both variants initialize the student from the original model.

sections.heading: Training data.
sections.text: We train separate mathematics and coding students using 3,200 prompts per domain from Skywork-OR1-RL-Data ( He et al., 2025 ) and KlearReasoner-CodeSub-15K ( Su et al., 2026 ) , respectively. Each original model generates four responses per prompt to form its own cached trajectories for self-distillation.

sections.heading: Benchmarks and metrics.
sections.text: We evaluate mathematical reasoning on AIME 2024, AIME 2025 ( Mathematical Association of America, 2026 ) , and HMMT 2025 ( Harvard–MIT Mathematics Tournament, 2025 ) , and code generation on LiveCodeBench (LCB) v5 and v6 ( Jain et al., 2025 ) . We report mean accuracy over 32 samples per mathematics problem (Avg@32) and four per coding problem (Avg@4).

sections.heading: Training and evaluation settings.
sections.text: We follow Lightning Weave’s offline DOPD training procedure ( Wu et al., 2026c ) , using a learning rate of 10 − 6 10^{-6} , global batch size 64, and distillation coefficient α = 2 \alpha=2 . Full training and evaluation settings are provided in Appendix A .

sections.heading: Comparison methods.
sections.text: We include published results from OPSD ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) , SDPO ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ) , PW-OPSD ( Liu et al., 2026 ) , and LOPD ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) for the corresponding models and benchmarks. These methods use reference solutions or feedback-conditioned self-teachers.

sections.heading: 4.2 Main Results
sections.text: Table 2 reports accuracy across five reasoning models and five mathematics and code benchmarks. The quantization and pruning variants of WISD improve average accuracy over the original models by 4.0 and 5.5 percentage points, respectively, with positive gains in 21 and 23 of the 25 model–benchmark settings. On both Qwen3-4B and OLMo-3-7B-Think, the two constructions improve the mathematics and code averages and are competitive with OPSD and SDPO. Both variants also surpass the reported five-benchmark averages of baselines that use privileged information. The largest gains occur on Qwen3.5-4B, where quantization and pruning increase the five-benchmark average by 11.3 and 13.4 points, respectively. In particular, pruning raises its HMMT 2025 accuracy from 57.7% to 70.5% and LCB v6 accuracy from 39.1% to 56.7%. The gains also extend to larger dense and MoE models, where pruning improves Qwen3.6-27B’s average accuracy by 5.2 points and quantization improves Qwen3.6-35B-A3B’s by 5.9 points. On the latter, HMMT 2025 and LCB v6 accuracies rise from 68.5% to 74.6% and from 61.8% to 69.5%, respectively. These results demonstrate that WISD turns simple weight degradation into effective self-distillation supervision, improving reasoning accuracy across model families, scales, and architectures without privileged information.

sections.text: We study quantization precision and pruning threshold using Qwen3.5-4B on HMMT25 (Avg@32), varying the hyperparameters b b and τ \tau to control the strength of quantization and pruning respectively while keeping all other settings the same as 4.1 . The sweeps cover b ∈ { 8 , 6 , 4 , 3 , 2 } b\in\{8,6,4,3,2\} and τ ∈ { 1 / 16 , 1 / 8 , 1 / 6 , 1 / 4 , 1 / 2 } \tau\in\{1/16,1/8,1/6,1/4,1/2\} . We report both student accuracy and average generated length. Figure 3 : Ablations of weak-model construction on Qwen3.5-4B, evaluated on HMMT25. (a) Quantization bit width. (b) Pruning threshold. Each pair shows accuracy (Avg@32, left plot) and average generated length in thousands of tokens (right plot). Dashed lines denote Base accuracy and average generated length. Outlined diamonds mark the default settings b = 3 b=3 and τ = 1 / 6 \tau=1/6 . Both constructions achieve their highest accuracy at intermediate weakening strengths. This pattern highlights the importance of balancing contrast strength and signal quality for effective self-distillation.

sections.heading: Quantization strength.
sections.text: Figure 3 (a) shows a non-monotonic relationship between weight precision and student accuracy. Reducing precision from 8 to 3 bits raises accuracy from 56.04% to 68.33%, while a further reduction to 2 bits lowers it to 49.90%. After self-distillation, the student also generates shorter responses than the Base model. This pattern suggests that mild quantization provides too little contrast for substantial gains over the original model, whereas excessive quantization erodes the weak model’s reasoning ability and allows noise to overwhelm useful contrast. Moderate quantization balances contrast strength and signal quality, with b = 3 b=3 giving the best result in this sweep and serving as our default.

sections.heading: Pruning threshold.
sections.text: Figure 3 (b) shows a similar intermediate range of effective constructions. Accuracy rises from 60.94% at τ = 1 / 16 \tau=1/16 to 69.38% at τ = 1 / 8 \tau=1/8 and 70.52% at the default τ = 1 / 6 \tau=1/6 , then falls to 54.79% and 49.58% at τ = 1 / 4 \tau=1/4 and 1 / 2 1/2 . After self-distillation, the student also generates shorter responses than the Base model. Similarly, the pruning results favor an intermediate level of damage that creates informative contrast while preserving the weak model’s reasoning ability. Our default threshold τ = 1 / 6 \tau=1/6 therefore combines the highest accuracy with the shortest responses in this sweep.

sections.heading: 5 Analysis
sections.text: We analyze the effectiveness of weak-model constructions and the resulting distillation signals on Qwen3-4B.

sections.heading: Alternative quantization and pruning methods.
sections.text: To evaluate the effectiveness of weak-model construction in providing contrast signals, we also explore alternative methods, including GPTQ ( Frantar et al., 2023 ) with 3-bit weights and W4A4 with and without SmoothQuant-style smoothing ( Xiao et al., 2023 ) for quantization, and Wanda-based pruning ( Sun et al., 2024 ) and SparseGPT ( Frantar and Alistarh, 2023 ) , both with a 2:4 sparsity pattern, for pruning. We train separate students for mathematics and code using the identical training settings in Section 4.1 . sections.text: To further assess the role of weight weakening, we consider two alternative training signals derived from the original model’s predictions. Self-enhancing directly uses the frozen original model’s token log-probabilities as rewards. Temperature weak softens the original model’s output distribution with a temperature of T = 2 T=2 , and uses the log-probability difference between the original and softened distributions as the reward. Implementation details are provided in Appendix A.5 . Table 3 shows the two confidence-based alternatives remain close to the original model. These results show that our quantization and pruning constructions provide effective, structured contrast signals for self-distillation, going beyond simply reinforcing the original model’s confidence and leading to improved reasoning capabilities. sections.heading: 5.2 Understanding the Training Signal
sections.text: We analyze how weak-model contrasts allocate supervision across reasoning roles on 64 Qwen3-4B mathematics training trajectories. We label response segments using the ThinkARM taxonomy ( Li et al., 2026a ) and measure each role’s share of the initial logit-gradient L1 magnitude. Table 4 shows that quantization and pruning allocate about 22% of the signal to exploration and 11% to verification, exceeding these roles’ token shares of 14.8% and 8.1%. Both constructions thus place greater training weight on exploring solution paths and checking intermediate reasoning. Appendix C provides the analysis details. Figure 4 illustrates how this supervision acts on tokens that support intermediate calculations and logical checks. In the paint-coverage example, quantization increases the target probabilities of a digit in the coverage calculation and the negation not , reinforcing the conclusion that the proposed amount of paint is insufficient. In the algebra example, pruning increases the target probability of 0 in an intermediate result, supporting the exclusion of a candidate root that makes the original divisor zero. These cases show how the contrast reinforces tokens that express numerical results and their logical consequences, supplying supervision for the local decisions that support correct reasoning.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced WISD, a self-distillation framework that improves reasoning models without privileged information. The core idea is to construct a weaker counterpart of the original model and turn their token-level log-probability contrast into dense supervision on self-generated trajectories. We instantiate this idea with low-bit quantization and magnitude pruning, enabling training from the original checkpoint and unlabeled prompts. Experiments across diverse reasoning models and benchmarks demonstrate broad accuracy gains. Our analyses show that weak-model contrasts emphasize exploration and verification while providing training directions beyond confidence reinforcement. These results establish model weakening as an effective source of supervision for improving reasoning through self-distillation.

sections.heading: Benchmarks and metrics.
sections.text: AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and HMMT 2025 each contain 30 problems, evaluated with 32 responses per problem. LiveCodeBench v5 and v6 contain 279 and 131 problems, respectively, evaluated with four responses per problem. Avg@ n n is the fraction of correct responses across all problems and their n n samples. Math Avg. equally weights the three mathematics benchmarks, Code Avg. equally weights the two coding benchmarks, and the final Avg. equally weights all five. We compute averages from unrounded scores. AIME 2024 also serves as the development benchmark for exploring weak-model constructions.

sections.heading: Generation settings.
sections.text: We use each model’s native chat template with thinking enabled, temperature 0.6 0.6 , top- p = 0.95 p=0.95 , and top- k k disabled. Our main-table evaluations use a 40,960-token output limit and a 49,152-token context window. Mean response length counts generated tokens, excluding the prompt.

sections.heading: Published results.
sections.text: OPSD and PW-OPSD mathematics results come from Table 4 of Liu et al. (2026) , with the Moderate schedule for PW-OPSD. These use Avg@12 averaged over three evaluation seeds, temperature 1.0 1.0 , top- p = 0.95 p=0.95 , and a 38,912-token output limit. Qwen3-4B SDPO mathematics results come from Table 1 of Wu et al. (2026a) , using pass@1 on the same LCB tasks, temperature 0.7 0.7 , top- p = 0.95 p=0.95 , top- k = 20 k=20 , and a 16,384-token output limit.

sections.heading: Mathematics prompt.
sections.text: Before application of the model’s native chat template, each mathematics example is represented exactly as Question: {Problem} Answer: We enable the model’s native reasoning mode where available and stop on its end-of-sequence or end-of-turn token. For every problem we independently sample 64 responses at temperature 0.6 and top- p = 0.95 p=0.95 , allowing at most 32,768 generated tokens. We extract the last balanced \boxed{...} expression, remove superficial formatting such as whitespace, delimiters, and units, and canonicalize integer answers before exact comparison with the reference. We do not use a computer-algebra system to grant additional symbolic equivalences. A length-truncated response is still scored if it contains a valid extracted answer.

sections.heading: LiveCodeBench prompt.
sections.text: We use LiveCodeBench’s CodeQwenInstruct generation format. Its user message begins with: You will be given a question (problem specification) and will generate a correct Python program that matches the specification and passes all tests. You will NOT return anything except for the program. Question: {question_content} For problems with starter code, the message then asks the model to complete the supplied code and enclose the answer in code delimiters. Otherwise it instructs the model to read from standard input, write to standard output, and return the program inside a Python code block initialized with # YOUR CODE HERE . The official system wrapper is You are a helpful assistant. , expressed with the Qwen instruction delimiters. We sample four responses per problem at temperature 0.6 and top- p = 0.95 p=0.95 , with a maximum of 40,960 generated tokens. We use LiveCodeBench’s official code extraction and test execution. A sample is correct only if its extracted program passes every test for that problem. Tests run in isolated, read-only containers with the benchmark’s fast-test mode and a six-second timeout per test. Runtime errors, timeouts, extraction failures, and incomplete programs are scored as incorrect.

sections.heading: Quantization.
sections.text: RTN uses symmetric group-wise quantization with 128 input coordinates per output-row group, except for the group-32 variant. The signed grid has 2 b − 1 2^{b}-1 levels, so 2-bit RTN uses { − 1 , 0 , 1 } \{-1,0,1\} . W4A8 and W4A4 combine 4-bit RTN weights with per-token activation quantization at 8 and 4 bits, respectively. Smooth W4A4 applies SmoothQuant-style input-channel and weight rescaling with smoothing exponent 0.5 0.5 before quantization ( Xiao et al., 2023 ) . GPTQ uses 3-bit or 2-bit weights, group size 128, and damping 0.01 0.01 ( Frantar et al., 2023 ) .

sections.heading: Pruning.
sections.text: Our default applies the group-relative threshold τ = 1 / 6 \tau=1/6 and restores each complete output row’s ℓ 2 \ell_{2} norm, as defined in Section 3.3 . The additional per-row magnitude variants remove the smallest 20% or 40% of weights in each row. Wanda ranks weights by magnitude times the clean-model input-activation norm, using either per-row sparsity or a 2:4 pattern ( Sun et al., 2024 ) . SparseGPT uses input covariance statistics with damping 0.01 0.01 , at 50% sparsity or with a 2:4 pattern ( Frantar and Alistarh, 2023 ) . MLP channel pruning removes the lowest-ranked 25% of channels according to the product of the down-projection column norm and its input-activation norm, jointly masking the corresponding gate/up rows and down columns.

sections.heading: Calibration and scoring.
sections.text: The calibrated alternatives use 128 cached training sequences from the corresponding domain, with up to 2,048 tokens per sequence. Calibration statistics are collected from the unchanged original model. GPTQ and SparseGPT accumulate and factorize their covariance matrices in FP64. The Qwen3-4B construction studies use FP32 scorer forwards and BF16 student training. The Qwen3.5-4B sweep uses BF16 scorers, except for the default pruning student, which uses the FP32-scored run from the main comparison. All constructions modify the frozen weak scorer and retain the student’s original architecture.

Analyze Explains a concept, builds a representation, or makes a logical deduction. Plan Commits to an action before carrying it out. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.38681v1 [cs.AI] 28 Oct 2026 Weaken to Strengthen: Weakening-Induced On-Policy Self-Distillation for Large Reasoning Models Yecheng Wu Affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology Correspondence to: wyc557@mit.edu Song Han Affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology Affiliation: NVIDIA Han Cai Affiliation: NVIDIA Abstract Self-distillation offers a way to improve reasoning models when a suitable external teacher is unavailable. However, common approaches rely on privileged information to construct a stronger self-teacher, limiting their use when only unlabeled prompts are available. In this paper, we introduce Weakening-Induced On-Policy Self-Distillation (WISD), which instead constructs a weaker counterpart of the original model and uses the contrast between the two as a training signal without requiring privileged information. We explore two ways to construct the weaker model: low-bit quantization and magnitude pruning. We evaluate WISD across diverse architectures and scales on mathematical and coding reasoning tasks. Across these benchmarks, quantization and pruning improve average accuracy over the original models by 4.0 and 5.5 percentage points, respectively, achieving state-of-the-art performance even without privileged information. Notably, pruning raises Qwen3.5-4B’s accuracy from 57.7% to 70.5% on HMMT 2025 and from 39.1% to 56.7% on LiveCodeBench v6. Quantization raises Qwen3.6-35B-A3B’s accuracy from 68.5% to 74.6% and from 61.8% to 69.5% on the same benchmarks, respectively. These results establish WISD as a novel and effective self-distillation framework for large reasoning models. Code is released at https://github.com/jet-ai-projects/WISD . Keywords: Self-Distillation, On-Policy Distillation, Reasoning, Large Language Models Figure 1 : Accuracy gains from self-distillation against a weakened model. By constructing a weakened copy of the original model and using the contrast between them as a training signal, WISD achieves consistent accuracy improvements across diverse reasoning models and benchmarks. Full results are reported in Table 2 . 1 Introduction On-policy distillation (OPD) has emerged as an effective approach to improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2024 ; Lu and Lab, 2025 ) . It trains a student on its own generated trajectories using dense token-level supervision from a teacher, combining learning on the student’s own states with fine-grained feedback. For reasoning tasks, this allows learning to address errors in intermediate computations and decisions along the student’s own solution paths. This approach has demonstrated substantial gains in training efficiency and is now used in the post-training of Qwen3, MiMo-V2-Flash, Nemotron-Cascade 2, and DeepSeek-V4 ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Team et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026d ; DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026 ) . Recent work extends OPD to self-distillation, in which the same model serves as both teacher and student, removing the need for a separate teacher model ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Shenfeld et al., 2026 ; Hübotter et al., 2026 ) . Self-distillation is particularly appealing when a suitable external teacher is unavailable, especially when the goal is to improve an already capable model ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ) . A common approach uses the model’s in-context learning ability to construct a stronger teacher by providing privileged information, such as reference solutions ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) , expert demonstrations ( Shenfeld et al., 2026 ) , or textual environment feedback ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ) . With this additional context, the teacher can provide more informed predictions for trajectories that the student generates from the task input alone. Training matches the student’s next-token distributions to the teacher’s, transferring the benefit of the richer context into a policy that operates without privileged information at inference time. However, these approaches retain a dependence on privileged information during training. Reference-based methods require solutions or expert demonstrations ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Shenfeld et al., 2026 ) , and obtaining high-quality solutions can be costly ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) . Feedback-based alternatives rely on informative environment responses or reward-verified successful rollouts ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ) . These requirements limit their applicability when only unlabeled prompts are available. Even when privileged information is available, conditioning on it can shift the teacher’s predictions away from the student’s and complicate knowledge transfer ( Penaloza et al., 2026 ) . This motivates our central question: Can a model improve its reasoning through self-distillation without privileged information? Recent work on weak-to-strong OPD shows that the log-probability contrast between paired models can provide useful supervision even when both are weaker than the student ( Feng et al., 2026 ; Yu et al., 2026 ) . Differences in token preferences between paired models encode a direction of policy improvement that can be transferred to a more capable student. From this perspective, the privileged-information approaches above take the model itself as the weaker member of a pair and construct a stronger counterpart through additional context ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Shenfeld et al., 2026 ; Hübotter et al., 2026 ) . We introduce Weakening-Induced On-Policy Self-Distillation (WISD), which reverses this construction: we take the original model as the stronger member and create a weaker counterpart by degrading its weights. The contrast between the original model and its weakened copy then provides dense supervision on the model’s own trajectories, without privileged information. This formulation turns model weakening into a source of supervision, enabling self-improvement using the original model and unlabeled task prompts alone. Table 1 compares WISD with representative reasoning post-training methods in terms of learning signals and external supervision requirements. Table 1 : Comparison of training methods for reasoning. WISD provides dense supervision without external teachers, reference solutions, or environment feedback. Reference solutions are externally supplied answers or worked solutions used as teacher context. Environment feedback includes outcome verification and textual responses. GRPO uses verifiable outcome rewards. SDPO uses textual feedback or reward-verified self-generated solutions. Method Dense Learning Signal No External Teacher No Reference Solutions No Environment Feedback GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) ✗ ✓ ✓ ✗ OPD ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ) ✓ ✗ ✓ ✓ OPSD ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) ✓ ✓ ✗ ✓ SDPO ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ) ✓ ✓ ✓ ✗ WISD (ours) ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Following this idea, we explore two training-free constructions of a weaker self: low-bit quantization and magnitude pruning. Both operate directly on model weights and require no calibration data. Experiments across diverse model architectures and scales demonstrate the effectiveness of WISD on mathematical and coding reasoning tasks. Figure 1 summarizes the gains in mathematical and coding reasoning. Across these benchmarks, quantization and pruning improve average accuracy over the original models by 4.0 and 5.5 percentage points, respectively, with positive gains in 21 and 23 of the 25 model–benchmark settings, achieving state-of-the-art performance even without privileged information. Notably, pruning raises Qwen3.5-4B’s accuracy from 57.7% to 70.5% on HMMT 2025 and from 39.1% to 56.7% on LiveCodeBench v6. Quantization raises Qwen3.6-35B-A3B’s accuracy from 68.5% to 74.6% and from 61.8% to 69.5% on the same benchmarks, respectively. These results establish WISD as a novel and effective self-distillation framework for large reasoning models, requiring minimal prerequisites. Our contributions are as follows: • We introduce WISD, a self-distillation approach that treats the original model as the stronger member of a pair and learns from its contrast with a weakened copy, improving reasoning without privileged information. • We instantiate this approach with two weak-model constructions, low-bit quantization and magnitude pruning, which require no calibration data and yield dense supervision on the model’s own trajectories. • We validate the approach across widely used reasoning models spanning diverse architectures and scales, demonstrating broad accuracy improvements on mathematical and coding reasoning tasks. 2 Related Work On-Policy Distillation. On-policy distillation trains a student on its own generated trajectories ( Li et al., 2026b ; Fu et al., 2026 ; Ruan et al., 2026 ) with token-level teacher feedback ( Jin et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Armandpour et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026b ) , reducing the distribution mismatch between training and inference ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2024 ; Lu and Lab, 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026b ; Xu et al., 2025 ) . Direct On-Policy Distillation (DOPD) and related approaches transfer policy shifts through log-probability contrasts between paired models ( Yang et al., 2026b ; Feng et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026c ) , enabling weak-to-strong distillation ( Yu et al., 2026 ) . A growing line of work extends OPD to self-distillation by conditioning the model itself on additional information to obtain a stronger teacher: reference solutions ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Ke et al., 2026 ; Shen et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026a ) , demonstrations ( Shenfeld et al., 2026 ) , and environment feedback or verified successful rollouts ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ; Tan and Hong, 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026c ; He et al., 2026 ; Sun et al., 2026 ) . Compared to these prior self-distillation approaches, WISD requires no privileged information. Instead, it constructs a weaker copy of the original model and uses the contrast between the two as the training signal. OPSA takes a complementary approach, constructing entropy-adaptive negative advantages without an external teacher or privileged information ( Ding and Zhang, 2026 ) . Learning from Weaker Models. Contrasting a model with a weaker counterpart has been explored for both generation ( Shi et al., 2024 ; Hong et al., 2023 ; Ahn et al., 2025 ) and learning. Contrastive decoding uses a smaller amateur to guide a stronger expert at inference time ( Li et al., 2023 ; O’Brien and Lewis, 2023 ) . Variants derive weaker predictions from the model itself ( Gera et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Jiang et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) through early layers in DoLa ( Chuang et al., 2024 ) , dropout or quantization in DCD ( Phan et al., 2024 ) , and layer pruning in PruneCD ( Yu et al., 2025 ) . Related small-model contrasts support decoding-time adaptation ( Mitchell et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) . In diffusion, classifier-free guidance contrasts conditional and unconditional predictions ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) , while autoguidance uses a smaller, less-trained counterpart ( Karras et al., 2024 ) . Training-time approaches include pruned self-competitors for visual representation learning ( Jiang et al., 2021 ) and expert–amateur contrasts for reasoning supervision ( Wang et al., 2026a ) . Recent distillation methods construct degraded references for flow-matching models ( Lin et al., 2026 ) or reduce expert activation in an external MoE teacher to obtain a reference ( Gu et al., 2026 ) . Self-distillation also exploits predictions conditioned on ablated visual inputs ( Liang et al., 2026 ) or self-generated negative context ( Pei et al., 2026 ) . WISD constructs a weaker counterpart directly through training-free weight quantization or magnitude pruning and distills its contrast with the original model to improve reasoning without privileged information. 3 Method We first review OPD and policy-shift supervision, then revisit self-distillation from a weak-to-strong perspective to introduce WISD. Finally, we describe two training-free ways to construct its weaker model. Figure 2 contrasts WISD with prior self-distillation and summarizes its training pipeline. Figure 2 : Overview of WISD. (a) Prior self-distillation. Privileged information c c , such as solutions, demonstrations, or feedback, strengthens the original model into a self-teacher. (b) WISD. We instead retain the original model as the stronger member and construct a weaker copy through training-free quantization or pruning. The frozen pair scores the same self-generated trajectories, and its token-level log-probability contrast provides cached supervision for a student initialized from the original model, without privileged information. 3.1 Preliminaries Let π θ \pi_{\theta} be an autoregressive student, x ∼ 𝒟 x\sim\mathcal{D} a prompt, and y ∼ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ x ) y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x) a generated response. OPD supervises the student on the states it visits during generation. Their token-level log-probability difference defines a policy shift: r ⁡ ( a ∣ s ) = log ⁡ π + ​ ( a ∣ s ) − log ⁡ π − ​ ( a ∣ s ) . r(a\mid s)=\log\pi^{+}(a\mid s)-\log\pi^{-}(a\mid s). The central design choice is therefore how to obtain a model pair whose relative predictions provide a learning signal. This paired-model perspective also offers a way to understand prior on-policy self-distillation (OPSD). Given a model π \pi and privileged information c c , these approaches construct a more informed self-teacher π ( ⋅ ∣ s , c ) \pi(\cdot\mid s,c) using reference solutions ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) , demonstrations ( Shenfeld et al., 2026 ) , or environment feedback ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ) . Viewed as a model pair, the original policy π ( ⋅ ∣ s ) \pi(\cdot\mid s) is the weaker member, while its context-conditioned counterpart is the stronger member. These two roles can be written as π − ​ ( a ∣ s ) = π ⁡ ( a ∣ s ) \pi^{-}(a\mid s)=\pi(a\mid s) and π + ​ ( a ∣ s ) = π ⁡ ( a ∣ s , c ) \pi^{+}(a\mid s)=\pi(a\mid s,c) . The student encounters the task without c c , and the additional context gives the teacher a more informed view of the student’s decisions. The construction therefore depends on additional information to create the gap from which the student learns. WISD reverses this construction: we take the original model as the stronger member and construct a weaker counterpart from its own weights. A token receives a positive contrast when it is more likely under the original model and a negative contrast when it is more likely under the weak model. This supplies dense self-supervision using only the original checkpoint and unlabeled prompts. A student initialized from θ 0 \theta_{0} is then trained on this supervision. The trajectories and both scoring models remain fixed throughout optimization. We evaluate WISD on five reasoning models: Qwen3-4B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , Qwen3.5-4B ( Qwen Team, 2026a ) , OLMo-3-7B-Think ( Team Olmo et al., 2026 ) , Qwen3.6-27B ( Qwen Team, 2026b ) , and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B ( Qwen Team, 2026c ) . These models span diverse sizes, families, and attention architectures, covering both dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) designs. For each model, we compare the original checkpoint with students trained using the quantization and pruning constructions in Section 3.3 , denoted by WISD (Quantization) and WISD (Pruning). The main results use b = 3 b=3 for quantization and τ = 1 / 6 \tau=1/6 for pruning. Both variants initialize the student from the original model. Training data. We train separate mathematics and coding students using 3,200 prompts per domain from Skywork-OR1-RL-Data ( He et al., 2025 ) and KlearReasoner-CodeSub-15K ( Su et al., 2026 ) , respectively. Each original model generates four responses per prompt to form its own cached trajectories for self-distillation. Benchmarks and metrics. We evaluate mathematical reasoning on AIME 2024, AIME 2025 ( Mathematical Association of America, 2026 ) , and HMMT 2025 ( Harvard–MIT Mathematics Tournament, 2025 ) , and code generation on LiveCodeBench (LCB) v5 and v6 ( Jain et al., 2025 ) . We report mean accuracy over 32 samples per mathematics problem (Avg@32) and four per coding problem (Avg@4). Training and evaluation settings. We follow Lightning Weave’s offline DOPD training procedure ( Wu et al., 2026c ) , using a learning rate of 10 − 6 10^{-6} , global batch size 64, and distillation coefficient α = 2 \alpha=2 . Full training and evaluation settings are provided in Appendix A . Comparison methods. We include published results from OPSD ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) , SDPO ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ) , PW-OPSD ( Liu et al., 2026 ) , and LOPD ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) for the corresponding models and benchmarks. These methods use reference solutions or feedback-conditioned self-teachers. 4.2 Main Results Table 2 reports accuracy across five reasoning models and five mathematics and code benchmarks. The quantization and pruning variants of WISD improve average accuracy over the original models by 4.0 and 5.5 percentage points, respectively, with positive gains in 21 and 23 of the 25 model–benchmark settings. On both Qwen3-4B and OLMo-3-7B-Think, the two constructions improve the mathematics and code averages and are competitive with OPSD and SDPO. Both variants also surpass the reported five-benchmark averages of baselines that use privileged information. The largest gains occur on Qwen3.5-4B, where quantization and pruning increase the five-benchmark average by 11.3 and 13.4 points, respectively. In particular, pruning raises its HMMT 2025 accuracy from 57.7% to 70.5% and LCB v6 accuracy from 39.1% to 56.7%. The gains also extend to larger dense and MoE models, where pruning improves Qwen3.6-27B’s average accuracy by 5.2 points and quantization improves Qwen3.6-35B-A3B’s by 5.9 points. On the latter, HMMT 2025 and LCB v6 accuracies rise from 68.5% to 74.6% and from 61.8% to 69.5%, respectively. These results demonstrate that WISD turns simple weight degradation into effective self-distillation supervision, improving reasoning accuracy across model families, scales, and architectures without privileged information. 4.3 Ablation Study We study quantization precision and pruning threshold using Qwen3.5-4B on HMMT25 (Avg@32), varying the hyperparameters b b and τ \tau to control the strength of quantization and pruning respectively while keeping all other settings the same as 4.1 . The core idea is to construct a weaker counterpart of the original model and turn their token-level log-probability contrast into dense supervision on self-generated trajectories. We instantiate this idea with low-bit quantization and magnitude pruning, enabling training from the original checkpoint and unlabeled prompts. Experiments across diverse reasoning models and benchmarks demonstrate broad accuracy gains. Our analyses show that weak-model contrasts emphasize exploration and verification while providing training directions beyond confidence reinforcement. A.3 Evaluation Prompts and Answer Extraction Mathematics prompt. Before application of the model’s native chat template, each mathematics example is represented exactly as Question: {Problem} Answer: We enable the model’s native reasoning mode where available and stop on its end-of-sequence or end-of-turn token. For every problem we independently sample 64 responses at temperature 0.6 and top- p = 0.95 p=0.95 , allowing at most 32,768 generated tokens. We extract the last balanced \boxed{...} expression, remove superficial formatting such as whitespace, delimiters, and units, and canonicalize integer answers before exact comparison with the reference. We do not use a computer-algebra system to grant additional symbolic equivalences. A length-truncated response is still scored if it contains a valid extracted answer. LiveCodeBench prompt. We use LiveCodeBench’s CodeQwenInstruct generation format. Its user message begins with: You will be given a question (problem specification) and will generate a correct Python program that matches the specification and passes all tests. You will NOT return anything except for the program. Question: {question_content} For problems with starter code, the message then asks the model to complete the supplied code and enclose the answer in code delimiters. Otherwise it instructs the model to read from standard input, write to standard output, and return the program inside a Python code block initialized with # YOUR CODE HERE . The official system wrapper is You are a helpful assistant. , expressed with the Qwen instruction delimiters. We sample four responses per problem at temperature 0.6 and top- p = 0.95 p=0.95 , with a maximum of 40,960 generated tokens. We use LiveCodeBench’s official code extraction and test execution. A sample is correct only if its extracted program passes every test for that problem. Tests run in isolated, read-only containers with the benchmark’s fast-test mode and a six-second timeout per test. Runtime errors, timeouts, extraction failures, and incomplete programs are scored as incorrect. A.4 Weak-Model Construction Details Quantization. RTN uses symmetric group-wise quantization with 128 input coordinates per output-row group, except for the group-32 variant. The signed grid has 2 b − 1 2^{b}-1 levels, so 2-bit RTN uses { − 1 , 0 , 1 } \{-1,0,1\} . W4A8 and W4A4 combine 4-bit RTN weights with per-token activation quantization at 8 and 4 bits, respectively. Smooth W4A4 applies SmoothQuant-style input-channel and weight rescaling with smoothing exponent 0.5 0.5 before quantization ( Xiao et al., 2023 ) . GPTQ uses 3-bit or 2-bit weights, group size 128, and damping 0.01 0.01 ( Frantar et al., 2023 ) . Pruning. Our default applies the group-relative threshold τ = 1 / 6 \tau=1/6 and restores each complete output row’s ℓ 2 \ell_{2} norm, as defined in Section 3.3 . The additional per-row magnitude variants remove the smallest 20% or 40% of weights in each row. Wanda ranks weights by magnitude times the clean-model input-activation norm, using either per-row sparsity or a 2:4 pattern ( Sun et al., 2024 ) . SparseGPT uses input covariance statistics with damping 0.01 0.01 , at 50% sparsity or with a 2:4 pattern ( Frantar and Alistarh, 2023 ) . MLP channel pruning removes the lowest-ranked 25% of channels according to the product of the down-projection column norm and its input-activation norm, jointly masking the corresponding gate/up rows and down columns. Calibration and scoring. The calibrated alternatives use 128 cached training sequences from the corresponding domain, with up to 2,048 tokens per sequence. Calibration statistics are collected from the unchanged original model. GPTQ and SparseGPT accumulate and factorize their covariance matrices in FP64. The Qwen3-4B construction studies use FP32 scorer forwards and BF16 student training. The Qwen3.5-4B sweep uses BF16 scorers, except for the default pruning student, which uses the FP32-scored run from the main comparison. All constructions modify the frozen weak scorer and retain the student’s original architecture.
